en: The Ritual Procedure for the Recitation and Practice of the Eight-Syllable Secret Dhāraṇī of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s Supreme Majestic Power:
I shall now explain this according to the gateway of the sequential method of mantras; first, the practitioner must receive it from an ācārya.
Having received the empowerment and the direct transmission, one enters once more into the empowerment for the *vidyādhara-siddhi*.

Endowed with compassionate conduct and the unconditional compassion that pities all sentient beings afflicted by suffering and calamity, one performs this recitation, vowing to protect all beings from fear and misfortune.
Whenever sentient beings encounter suffering and hardship, whether at their location or through incense...

One may construct an altar by smearing it with ointments or kneading powders together; however, for those who practice constant recitation, it is necessary to have a purified chamber and establish a *maṇḍala* according to the Dharma, as prescribed in all the preceding methods.
Before practicing the Dharma, the practitioner must first give rise to eight kinds of mental states: first, the mind of compassion; second, the stainless mind;
third, the mind free from the notion of "mine"; fourth, the mind free from attachment to superiority; fifth, the mind of equanimity.
Sixth, one should have a mind free from enmity and harm; seventh, one should have a mind of compassion; eighth, one should have a mind free from greed for gain.
A person such as this may transmit and receive [the rite] from others. If one is not of such a nature, one should perform it alone so that the rite may be successfully accomplished.
If the prescribed number of recitations has not yet been completed, one must not suddenly converse with another person in the interim, thereby causing an interruption. If...
If the ritual has not yet been performed, one must first clearly announce it. Even when performing recitations oneself, one must not allow them to be interrupted.

When the practitioner enters the maṇḍala, they should perform a reverent prostration and, with vajra-palms joined, visualize with focused intent all the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Great Sage Mañjuśrī, the immeasurable bodhisattvas, and Vajrapāṇi.
Before the assembly of noble sages and others, one bows with each individual body to the holy multitude, universally prostrating to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vajras.
The mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) sarva-tathāgata-kāya-vāk-citta (2) va (3).
Vajrapramardin (4) Mañjuśrī-vāgīśvarāya (5). Furthermore, the heart-mantra is as follows:
Oṃ vajra-vitta-saṃhata. Joining the vajra-palms, with the ten fingers interlaced outwardly, let the five wheels [fingers] all touch the ground;
with utmost sincerity and reverence, perform prostration. Then, kneeling with the right knee on the ground, join the palms as if forming a lotus bud.
Visualize the body as a crystal; the syllable HŪṂ is at the three places.
Imagine it becoming the five-pronged vajra, the so-called inner vajra, which is an indestructible essence.
Then, with sincere devotion, invite all the holy deities and recite these four lines of verse.
I prostrate to the Unsurpassed King of Physicians of Dharma, The Compassionate Lord who can save those difficult to teach.
I now take refuge and respectfully entreat you: I pray only that you will swiftly descend to this place of practice.
Thus, having made this threefold request, one makes the following formal declaration: With both hands joined in the lotus mudrā, [one says:]
Furthermore, recite the mantra for purifying the three karmas to render the vessel of the body pure.
Use it to consecrate the five places—the forehead, the two shoulders, the heart, and the throat—reciting that mantra as follows: Oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’ham.
Having purified the three karmas through the *mūṃ* [syllable],
one binds the Buddha-samaya mudrā: join the palms of concentration and wisdom like a lotus, open and close the two fire-peaks (*jvālā-śikhara*),
bend the upper joints of the two wind-fingers (*vāyu-aṅguli*), and pinch the roots of the wind-fingers with the two space-fingers (*ākāśa-aṅguli*).
Place the seal before the forehead and contemplate all Buddhas clearly and distinctly,
seeing them each dwelling in the midst of space. Recite that mantra,
which is the Samaya of the Buddha Family.
With the hands joined in the inner fist of samādhi and wisdom, the two thumbs are both held upright.

Contemplate all Buddhas as if they were right before one’s eyes; then, summoning the Honored One according to the visualization, join the two fists together and recite the mantra for the simultaneous invocation:
Oṃ e nika svāhā (recite three or seven times). Again, bind the secret samaya mudrā of the Padma family; its form is also as before: insert the left hand and extend the right.
Recite three times and invoke three times, then place the right hand and scatter [the offerings].
Recite that mantra:
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā. Furthermore, for the Vajra Family, the mudrā of the subtle samādhi is formed by modifying the previous mudrā’s empty wheel (the thumbs).
Insert the right hand into the left and extend the fingers upward in a beckoning gesture;
with single-minded concentration, recollect the Honored One. Recite that mantra: Oṃ Vajradhṛk Svāhā. The mudrā of the Buddha Family is placed upon the forehead;
the Lotus [Family] is at the right ear; the Vajra [Family] is at the left ear.

Next, for the Armor Mudrā (*kavaca-mudrā*), scatter [the fingers] over the crown of the head. Interlace the *dāna* (thumb) and *prajñā* (forefinger) with the *śīla* (ring finger) and *dik* (little finger), placing them inside the palms so that the tips of the *kṣānti* (middle finger) and *praṇidhāna* (index finger) touch.
Bend the *vīrya* (third finger) like a hook and place it externally behind the two *tejas* (thumbs).
The wisdom and dhyāna [mudrās] are held straight up like a vajra. Visualize [it] added to five places on the body:
the forehead, the right shoulder, the left [shoulder], the heart, and the throat, spreading to the crown of the head. Recite that mantra: Oṃ krodha-vajra-kīlita-prakṣepaya tāḥ.
NĀRĀ NĀRAVĀSA MANDALU HŪṂ SVĀHĀ. Next, the vajra-ground-boundary-kīla-mudrā is taught.
Form the mudrā of concentration with the palms joined in the vow of deliverance; enter the gate of morality and patience with both hands.
Then, secretly intertwining them behind the gate of morality, place them within the interval of the gate of generosity. Form the vow by intertwining them to enter the gates of patience and diligence.

Let generosity, wisdom, diligence, power, meditation, and knowledge each join their respective counterparts. Rotate three times downward and press the thumbs together. Then recite the mantra as follows:
Oṃ kili kili vajravajri phuru phuraṃda phaṭ. Furthermore, the Vajra-Boundary-Seal (Vajraprākāramudrā) is taught.

Following the previous earth-boundary mudrā: extend the *citta-jñāna* (middle finger) and raise the *dhyāna-jñāna* (ring finger), turning them clockwise like a wall or courtyard while reciting the mantra.
Visualize a vajra wall. Recite the mantra: Oṃ sara sara vajraprākāra hūṃ phaṭ.
Furthermore, within the Ākāśagarbha [maṇḍala], the ten pāramitās interlace one another.
Through the power of diligence, by forming the perception of jewels, a wondrous pavilion is established; atop it is a great lotus flower.
With a concentrated mind, visualize the deity residing within a jeweled canopy, surrounded on all sides by banners, streamers, parasols, celestial garments, and clouds of incense like a vast ocean.
Pervading the entirety of space, surrounded by his retinue, he recites this mantra:
Oṃ gaganasvabhāvaviśuddha hūṃ. Next, perform the chariot mudrā: interlace the fingers of the wisdom and concentration hands with palms facing upward, pressing the right hand over the left.
With the wisdom and dhyāna fingers joined at the forefinger, place the little finger of the lower hand beneath;
rotate it forward and visualize it as becoming a precious chariot. Recite this mantra: Oṃ avalokitu hūṃ.
Three or seven times, visualize the Honored One mounting his carriage and slowly descending to the site of practice;
remaining in mid-air, he awaits the invitation to enter, never failing his original vow. Recite the mantra as follows:
Namo siddhyādhipataye tathāgatāya. Oṃ vajra-jīva-āgaccha svāhā.
By the power of this mantra and through the application of mudrās,
one is able to summon the principal deity along with his retinue to descend upon the site of practice. To bestow blessings upon the practitioner,
when intending to form the chariot [mudrā], one should first purify the path and hold an incense burner with both hands.
Meditate upon the secret mantra to purify the path through space;
thereafter, invite the Honored Sage, visualizing that the incense reaches his palace. Recite this mantra: Oṃ susiddhikari-jvalitānalamūladaye.
JVALA MATA MATA HANA HŪṂ PHAṬ. If one performs this sublime rite, the locks of the sky will all open of their own accord;
it also accomplishes the warding off of obstacles, as well as purification and so forth, and brings about the awakening of the Honored One.
Together with their retinues and those who attend them, first perform the invitation.
Following the mudrās and reciting the subsequent vidyā, summon all the noble ones to enter within the maṇḍala.
The mantra for summoning and inviting is recited either three or seven times to call them into the ritual site; then, respectfully present the request.
Furthermore, invite Mañjuśrī, Guhyakapāda, and Vajrapāṇi. Join the palms of wisdom and concentration like a lotus; twist the fire-wheels (the ring fingers) together.

At the tips of the peaks (the thumbs), press the backs of the nails. Bend the two wind-fingers (the index fingers) so they touch each other, and join the two space-fingers (the little fingers) upright.
Press the wind-patterns against the peaks of the space-fingers. Recite the secret mantra three times to summon them.
Namo samantabuddhānām. He he kumāra-kavimuktī-patā-siddhe samara samara pratyakṣiṇa svāhā.
Furthermore, as for the Family Vidyārājas who dispel all obstacles: join the palms of concentration and wisdom like lotuses;
let the water and wind fingers hang down together, both entering the space between the full moons.
With the empty fingers separated from the wind joints, recite the vidyā-mantra at the heart seven times while raising the forehead level. Turning to the left performs the rite of expulsion.
Forming a boundary by circling to the right, he drives away all obstructors without hindrance.
His majestic radiance is like the fire at the end of an eon; he is wrathful and inspires great terror.
He has three faces and six arms, wielding a vajra, a vase, a lotus, and a rosary.
Oṃ (1) duna duna (2) marta marta (3) hana hana (4) haya giri-ba hūṃ phaṭ. Furthermore,
the heart-mantra is as follows:
Oṃ āmlīkṣuṇa phaṭ (with a short *pha*). By means of this mantra and the empowerment of the mudrā, all obstacles are removed;
with but a small effort, the practitioner swiftly attains accomplishment.
Furthermore, to bind the higher realms, perform the *vajra-jāla* (Vajra Net) mudrā:
as with the previous wall-seal, open the space and pinch the base of the wind-fingers; place them flat on top to cover it.
Recite the mantra seven times while adding the seal tightly, rotating it to the right three times according to the ritual dance, and finally release the fingers to let them hang downward.
Visualize a canopy that covers the entire realm, extending from the walls down to the ground;
nothing can pierce it, as it becomes as solid as a vajra. Recite this mantra: Oṃ viśvavajrapañjara.
[Go] Phaṭ (half-syllable). Next is the Seal of the Fire Court:
The flames are sewn together in secret, radiating brilliant light; A surrounding net encircles it, blazing like the fierce fire at the end of an aeon;
It swirls to the right like the wind, reaching out to terrify all evil māras.
No one at all shall be able to cause harm or affliction.
The practitioner, remaining firm and maintaining the visualization, recites this mantra: Oṃ āsaṃgini hūṃ phaṭ.

Recite three or seven times while visualizing the empowerment; Contemplate the light-flames within the visualization, shimmering and blazing with brilliant radiance, Causing all dharmas to be accomplished without fail. Furthermore, clearly offer the arghya water;
visualize the concentration and wisdom hands both opened upward, With the earth, water, and fire fingers joined at their tips, And the wind fingers bent like a conch shell (śaṅkha).

With the two middle fingers grasping the wind-element below, visualize it as becoming a pond of various jewels, its bottom clear and filled with golden sand. Recite this mantra: *Namo samantabuddhānāṃ ākāśasamāsama*.
Recite *svāhā* three or seven times.
Visualize that within a jeweled pond, lotus buds and blossoms open to bathe all the noble assemblies.
First, bathe the feet of the Principal Deity; next, bathe all the other sages and holy ones.
Furthermore, bathing the assembly of noble deities, may my sense faculties and their objects be purified.
Next, regarding the lion throne, its mudrā is as explained below: Interlace the earth and water fingers, inserting them into the palms;
join the two fire fingers, standing their tips upright; bend the wind fingers to pinch the two space fingers; and extend the two space fingers together, facing forward.
With the posture of a lion’s stride, visualize a lotus flower above; recite that mantra:
Oṃ ājñāvilaya. Then perform the universal offering. Join the ten fingers like a vajra; the two wind-fingers [the thumbs] are in the shape of a jewel.
With incense, flowers, food, and lamps, one should visualize them as vast as clouds and oceans;
with banners, streamers, various musical instruments, flower canopies, and exquisite celestial garments, they are scattered throughout all of space. Offering this increases the accumulation of merit.
"Food" refers to the words of the mantra, which are used to present offerings to the Honored Ones. The mantra for making offerings is: [Mantra follows]
Namo samantabuddhānām | Oṃ sarvathā khaṃ unnaṭe sphāra-mukha gaganakhaṃ svāhā | By means of this offering,
one shall obtain incomparable benefit and be able to accomplish all activities.
The provisions arise from this. Next, the praise is explained: without releasing the previous mudrā, one changes the *ratna* [mudrā] and interlaces them.
Reciting the praise in the Sanskrit language, one causes the assembly of noble ones to rejoice and recites this secret mantra:
Oṃ vajratikṣṇa mahāyana vajraghoṣa mahāyudha mañjuśrī vajranirbhāsi vajramuṣṭi.
Namo Ratnatrayāya (4). Furthermore, there is a great praise in the Chinese language:
I take refuge in the Lord of Secret Activity, The subduer of all māras, The youthful Dharma Prince.
Possessing the myriad practices of Samantabhadra, Abiding in this primordially existent body,
With beginningless and endless quiescent, wondrous activity, he grants all vows; Subduing enmity and harm, and the three poisons,
He practices through the transformation of kalpas, and within the triple world, Reiterates the secret mantra teachings To protect the classes of sentient beings.

Establishing the gate of great skillful means, To utterly rescue all sentient beings, Causing them to transcend the wheel of birth and death, And enter from the stage of ordinary beings into the Buddha-ground.
The practitioner speaks these words, Praising and chanting for the Honored One;
Reciting with a sincere heart three times, Causing the Great Sage to rejoice, So that the practitioner’s sought-after vows may be fulfilled.
All shall be swiftly perfected. Furthermore, the Noble Mañjuśrī: For the mudrā of the Invoking Youth, form a fist with the hands;
extend the wind-finger (the index finger) in the shape of a hook. Recite three times after seven invocations, and then speak the mantra as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām akṣayāya svāṃ kuru āraṃ kumāryai svāhā. Furthermore, as for the *kṣetranī* mudrā, its form is as described below:
form a fist with the wisdom hand (*prajñāhasta*).
Fire and wind are joined vertically, because they share the same characteristic as the blade of a sword. Recite that secret mantra:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ | He he kumāri ke | Jyeṣṭhe nande śame śama-pratīcchane svāhā || 2 ||
Furthermore, to the right of the Honored One is the Youthful Protector Prajñākumāra.
With his left hand in the vajra-fist, he sits upright with it resting at his side; his right hand extends the five fingers straight upward to cover his heart.
Pressing firmly against the space-element (ākāśadhātu), one should recite this mantra:
Namo samantabuddhānām (1) He mahā-mahā (2) samalapraticire svāhā upakeśini. Forming a fist with the wisdom hand, extend the fire-wheel (middle finger) straight.
The Vāyu [mudrā]: bend the fingers at the middle joints so that they resemble the points of halberds. Recite this mantra:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ (1) Lūnaye khiraṇe (2) He kumārīke (3) Svāhā. (4)
Furthermore, O Jālinīprabha, the inner retinue consists of youths; their mudrās are as described below:
form a fist with the hand of samādhi and extend the wind-wheel (the little finger) like a hook.
To gather all sentient beings and establish them on the ground of liberation, he then spoke this mantra:
Namo samantabuddhānām. Hī hī kumārakumārabhūtāya svabhāvavicitrāya svāhā. Furthermore, the banner of the Wisdom of the Earth (Kṣitigarbha):
it is the emblem of his inner retinue; the hand of Samādhi forms a fist.
Then, spreading out the earth and water wheels, one should stand upright with the *dhvaja* (banner) and *cihna* (emblem) joined;
recite this secret mantra: *Namo samantabuddhānām | He samara kīraṇa ketu | Svāhā* || 1 || [1] *Svāhā* || 2 || *Kīraṇa-ketu* || 3 || *Bhava-ha* || 4 ||
Next, furthermore, for Vimalaprabha and Kumbhāṇḍa, the Lord of Secrets:
as before, extend the samādhi-hand upward with all fingers, then fully bend them inward.
Like the radiance of the Buddha’s body, its flames shine forth with intense brilliance. Recite his mantra, saying:
Namo samantabuddhānām (1). Hī hī kumāravicitrāgrye kumāramanusmara svāhā (2). Furthermore, for the inconceivable wisdom seal, the hand gestures are as described below:
interlace the fingers of the hands of meditative concentration and wisdom within.
First, form the fist-mudrā; second, extend the wind-fingers separately. Bend the two joints and bring them together so that the nails are pressed tightly against one another.
Extend the two thumbs side by side and hold them upright. This is called the Fist-instruction.
Furthermore, the Teacher spoke this secret mantra:
Namo samantabuddhānām (1) hī hī kiṃjirāye āviśāsmāyanaye svāhā. At that time, the practitioner, abiding in a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, acts for the sake of all sentient beings.
Having made the great, universal vow, With utmost sincerity, one should arouse deep reverence.
Visualize the deity emitting golden light, Seated upon a lion throne, Wielding the sword of wisdom in the right hand and holding a blue lotus in the left;
Upon the center of the flower stands a wisdom-vajra, And at the crown of the head is the Lord of Eight Wisdoms.
Its radiant light pervades the ten directions, as if facing the eyes of the practitioner. The fundamental mudrā of Mañjuśrī is to be received from the teacher in secret.
Next, one should take up the rosary; resting it within the palms, the hands of concentration and wisdom are joined in the lotus gesture.
One should then perform the empowerment with the mouth using the Secret Bead Mantra, which says:
Oṃ vairocana-maṇi svāhā. Having empowered [the rosary] seven times, rotate the beads three times for every thousand recitations.
While facing an empty space, hold the beads between the thumb and forefinger and move them three times in accordance with the recitation.
Recite the eight-syllable mantra one thousand or ten thousand times.
Recite each syllable clearly and distinctly, sitting upright and contemplating them with focused attention.
Without allowing even a single thought-moment to be interrupted, when the counting is finished, abide in the wisdom of observation.
Together with the gateway of samādhi, visualize the syllables as seed-syllables within a full moon; or perform the visualization of Mahāvairocana—the circular radiance is likewise so.
Dedicating all merits to all sentient beings, May they all attain the path of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, to explain the specific details: At three or four sessions, Ensure that there is no regression.
If for the purpose of pacifying calamities, One must begin at night; If seeking the gateway of merit and wisdom, [one should begin at dawn].
Rising at the beginning of the latter part of the night, one subdues [the deity] at solar noon. When desiring sleep through love and respect, the hook-summoning is likewise as before.
Having completed the recitation, one returns the jewel-seal (maṇi-mudrā), which is also identical to the ritual for *siddhi*.
Once the count of the principal deity is finished, one recites for the inner retinue as before; the eight deities follow their former sequence.
Praise and offer incense and flowers; present the *argha* water twice again.
Make the aspiration and the request, then dissolve the boundary and use the fire court to dismiss and escort [the deities].
Perform the protection of the body for the three families again, donning the armor as was done at the beginning. Yamāntaka provides the guard, and the great sword is empowered by touch.
Having paid homage to the multitude of noble sages, one may wander at will. Whether dwelling among mountains and forests,
practicing the dhūta austerities in the wilderness, encountering royal peril or imprisonment, facing sudden calamities and terrors,
suffering from disease or the afflictions of spirits, walking in fear through the dark night, or being harassed by Māra while cultivating the Path— [in all such times, one should remain steadfast].
In families prone to strife and discord, when various poisons and desires come to cause harm, one should constantly maintain the eight secret mantras as previously described;
there is no evil that they will not utterly eradicate. Regarding the various gateways of mudrās, one must receive them secretly from a master.
If one is within a maṇḍala, one may freely [perform them] directly before the Honored One.
Yawning, moving the limbs and joints, sighing, blowing, shaking the head, making foul sounds in the throat,
spitting, making noise, and coughing— such matters as these should be restrained; one must not be arrogant toward the Great Teacher, the Ācārya,
who practices deeply and possesses skillful wisdom, if one desires to seek great *siddhi*.
One must perform homa frequently, each time completing three lakṣas. When performing the fire offering once,
if the three signs appear— warmth, smoke, and light— and if from within the sword there arise a great sound like the Brahma-voice or a lion’s roar,
or a subtle resonance like thunder, or the elegant sound of bells, drums, and song;
Through various sounds of the Dharma teachings, the practitioner attains *siddhi*. One should perform the *homa* according to the instructions, understanding them with subtle clarity.
Even if minor details are inconsistent, when three hundred thousand recitations are completed, all evils will gather [and vanish].
One will constantly behold Mañjuśrī and attain liberation through the gateway of mental penetration.
Wisdom is unfathomable; May all aspirations for the mundane and supramundane worlds Be fully satisfied.
The Eight-Character Ritual of Mañjuśrī.
On the thirtieth day of the eighth month in the fourth year of the Changqing era, by the śramaṇa Yiyun of the East Pagoda Cloister at Qinglong Monastery.
Dharmavajra and the Tripitaka Master Bodhisattva from Central India translated the text together;
the verses were finalized and the prose polished by the monk Yiyun, who recorded this at the conclusion of the collation.
